title: Search a 2D Matrix: binary search on flattened or top-right elimination.
shortTitle: Search a 2D Matrix: binary search on a conceptually flattened grid
keyPoints: A globally sorted matrix is a sorted array folded into rows, so one binary search finds any value in O(log(m*n)) time.
Map a 1D index to 2D coordinates: row = mid / cols, col = mid % cols.
The search range is low = 0 and high = m * n - 1 over the conceptual flattened array.
Use the overflow-safe midpoint: mid = low + (high - low) / 2.
This approach only works when the first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row.
For row-sorted-only matrices (no row chaining), use top-right corner elimination in O(m + n) time.
Space complexity is O(1) for both approaches.

s1_definition.oneliner: A fully sorted matrix is just a sorted array folded into rows, so one binary search with index mapping finds any value in logarithmic time.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Globally sorted matrix** – rows are sorted left to right and the first element of each row exceeds the last element of the previous row.
- **Flattened view** – the matrix is conceptually one sorted array of length m * n, folded into rows.
- **Index mapping** – convert a 1D index to 2D: `row = mid / cols` and `col = mid % cols`.
- **Single binary search** – search the range [0, m*n - 1] in O(log(m*n)) time.
- **Top-right elimination** – an alternative for row-sorted-only matrices, walking from the top-right corner in O(m + n) time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India prints a giant ledger where every page has transaction amounts sorted smallest to largest, and the last amount on page one is always smaller than the first amount on page two. Rajesh wants to know if an amount of exactly fifty thousand rupees appears anywhere. Instead of reading every page, he treats all pages as one long sorted list, jumps to the middle, and decides whether to look in the earlier half or the later half.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Searching a sorted 2D matrix exploits the fact that a globally sorted matrix is just a sorted array folded into rows. Because reading row by row gives one long non-decreasing sequence, a single binary search over the conceptual flattened array of length `m * n` finds any value in O(log(m*n)) time.

The technique that makes this work is the index mapping: a 1D midpoint converts to `row = mid / cols` and `col = mid % cols`. The rest is standard binary search with the overflow-safe midpoint form.

For matrices where each row and column is sorted but rows do not chain together, the flattened approach does not work. Instead, start from the top-right corner and eliminate one row or column per step, giving O(m + n) time.

In a banking system at the National Bank of India, the end-of-day settlement report stored as a globally sorted grid benefits from the flattened binary search, answering compliance queries in a handful of comparisons even on grids with millions of entries.

Remember one sentence: a globally sorted matrix is a folded sorted array, so map 1D indices to 2D with division and modulo and run one binary search.
